newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN draws up plan in case of exodus from Iraq.
newsitem.headline: UN draws up plan in case of exodus from Iraq.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said on Tuesday it was drawing up contingency plans in case of a refugee exodus from Iraq, but so far saw no signs of mass movements of civilians.

UNHCR staff in Baghdad, the northern Iraqi city of Arbil and in Sulaymaniya reported the towns were calm despite U.S. missile strikes on southern Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds in the north.
But the Geneva-based agency expressed concern over the lack of water in Arbil -- a potential health risk which could drive people to flee the city.
"They have set up this task force just specifically to watch this unfolding situation in Iraq in case there are large-scale movements," UNHCR spokesman Ron Redmond told a news briefing.
"So far, we see no evidence of that," he added.

UNHCR, whose mandate does not normally cover internally displaced persons, is looking after 4,000 Iranian Kurd refugees scattered around northern Iraq as well as 14,000 Turkish Kurd refugees in Atrush camp in the north.
The task force includes the head of UNHCR's Middle East bureau and officials from the emergency section and Iraq desk.
They will review UNHCR's stocks of essential survival goods in the region, including those in Turkey, and evaluate whether more staff should be deployed.
As with any emergency, they will also draw up contingency plans should it become necessary to evacuate the six international staff if they are in danger.
"In Iraq as a whole we have 20 staff," UNHCR spokesman Rupert Colville told Reuters. "None of them are Americans."

The northern town of Arbil is held by Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) guerrillas after Iraqi KDP irregular forces and Iraqi national forces threw out the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) at the weekend.
"There was not a large-scale exodus out of Arbil even when the Iraq-KDP forces came in," Redmond said.
However, KDP officials have accused the PUK in Sulaymaniya of cutting water and electricity into Arbil.
"People are going about their normal busines in Arbil. But there is no electricity or water. It could get very serious," Colville told Reuters.
